chapter_theme: On the eve of her wedding the maiden prays at the Jina's feet, goes to her terrace and sees the stars, and her friends speak of love and the drum of tomorrow; then the night passes over the city, from the setting moon to the sleep of the revellers, spirits and birds.

cast.role: the bride-to-be of the wedding sarukkam, unnamed in these verses
her circle of friends, each speaking as 'ஒருத்தி' (one of them)
the young men of the city
the spirits that roam at night
the cock birds of the grove

1039.reading: The poet says that lotuses clustered at the feet of the lord of the wheel of grace seem to spread shade, fragrance and petals, and asks whether the bright joy of those whose minds are set on action is a matter of words.
1039.nuance: The stanza was printed as eight half-lines, and lines 2 and 3 are near-repeats of one another; the sentence is left unfinished or broken, so the figure of the lotuses at the Lord's feet is the only part held with some confidence.

1040.reading: The maiden praises the Jina's red feet with many humble words and prays that the disease of birth leave her.
1040.nuance: The prayer for release comes on the eve of her wedding and is soon set beside the friends' talk of love, which one of them (1049) ranks above release.
1040.event: The maiden hails the Jina's feet and prays that the sickness of birth depart.

claims.claim: birth is a disease from which a person asks to be freed

1041.reading: Having bowed to the victor's feet she goes slowly to the golden mansion of her rich city and reaches the courtyard of its moonlit terrace, her desire newly budded.
1041.nuance: The desire named in the last line sets the mood of the whole night that follows.
1041.event: The maiden leaves her worship, walks to her mansion and reaches the moonlit terrace court.

1042.reading: As the red sun draws in his rays and the evening sky slowly darkens, the white crescent that the world worships rises from the ocean.

1043.reading: Stars crowd the pale sky like flowers spread over a deep pool, and the maiden looks at them as they seem to spill a bright smile.
1043.nuance: The sky is called pale (பசலை), the lover's own word for her sickness, so the heavens already wear her colour.
1043.event: The maiden gazes at the first stars of the evening sky.

1044.reading: The maiden thinks that the star has joined the moon, her husband, and shows a budding smile, so that this is the hour of a wedding and the pleasure of youth is for the young.
1044.nuance: Her thought is a comparison of herself with the star, whose name (தாரகை) is also the common word for a star; the verse does not name her.
1044.event: The maiden reads the star and moon as a bride and groom and longs for her own union.

1045.reading: Her young lover's image stirring within, she tries to hide the sickness in her heart, but the gold-spreading pallor of her body tells that this is the sickness of desire.
1045.nuance: The verse puts her wish to hide beside the body's betrayal, which is the way Tamil love poetry usually shows desire.
1045.event: The maiden tries to hide her longing, and her pallor gives it away.

1046.reading: Her circle of friends, with bamboo-like arms, see her inner mood and softly speak many gentle words to her.
1046.event: The friends read the maiden's hidden mood and speak gently to her.

1047.reading: One sweet-spoken friend says that the earth, with its swelling waters and cloud-touched groves, is sweeter than the world of the Vidyadharas, and speaks to the doll-like maiden at her side.
1047.nuance: That a Vidyadhara maiden should be told the earth is sweeter hints at a bride from one world to be married into another; the verse does not say so, and the lines are clipped.
1047.event: A friend tells the maiden that the earth is lovelier than the Vidyadharas' world.

1048.reading: Another friend says that the cool hillside and the seasonal grove hurt the lonely, but wherever the loved one agrees to be, no distress comes.
1048.nuance: Line 2 is hard to parse, so only its general sense, that the lonely are hurt by pleasant scenery, is taken.
1048.event: A second friend tells the maiden that the beloved's company removes all distress.

1049.reading: A friend says that if lovers' love mingles so that neither is a stranger to the other, even the state without death and birth should be taken as husk.
1049.nuance: The claim is a friend's lover's boast in a love scene; a Jain work would not teach it as doctrine, and the verse sits eight verses after the maiden's own prayer to be free of birth.
1049.event: A third friend tells the maiden that the love of a united pair outweighs even release.

claims.claim: the union of loving partners is worth more than the state of release from death and birth

1050.reading: Without their mates the birds of the pond are like a fire to the separated, and no one will come to speak for women left alone by their husbands.
1050.nuance: The reading rests on the uncertain syntax of lines 1-2: the pond and the bird parted from its mate are taken as a figure of separation, but the word division is doubtful.

1051.reading: The breeze that mixes the scent of mullai and jasmine, the evening and the young moon's beams are said to waste the slender women.
1051.nuance: The friends build a list of the evening's agents of torment, as the poets of love always do, though the maiden is not yet parted from anyone.

1052.reading: One friend says that she heard in the crowded street a drum proclaiming that the maiden's wedding rite will be held tomorrow.
1052.nuance: The speaker is taken to be a friend by the same use of ஒருத்தி as in 1047 to 1049; the line division is clipped.
1052.event: A friend tells the maiden that the wedding drum has been sounded for tomorrow.

1053.reading: A speaker says that tomorrow is very far, and with eyes brimming proposes to bow at the cool white moon's feet and ask something of it.
1053.nuance: What is asked of the moon is lost in the lines' broken grammar, and the speaker may be the maiden herself speaking through her friends.

1054.reading: The speaker says that Kama has had the use of his arrows through the eyes, that this is the day to enjoy good deeds, and asks whether they may go to the Jina's city for a boon as the night watches pass.
1054.nuance: The word வாமன் has appeared for the Jina in 1040; here the identity of the city and of the speaker is not fixed, so the reading is held loosely.

claims.claim: a day of joy is the day on which earlier good deeds are enjoyed as their fruit

1055.reading: After such laughing talk in the company of her friends, the swan-gaited maiden climbs onto her fragrant bed as the king's seven-note instruments sound.
1055.event: The maiden joins her friends' talk, hears the royal music and goes to her scented bed.

1056.reading: When the jasmine-scented evening has passed and the instruments are still, the moon's milky rays slowly shrink and the young white moon sinks beyond the swelling sea.

1057.reading: As good deeds pass away and the harassing evil deeds come in, so the darkness thickens, and the many acts stop; the night belongs only to those of strong evil deeds.
1057.nuance: The karma saying is used as a figure for darkness, not as the verse's subject; it recalls the saying that a spent store of merit lets evil enter, and the poet gives it without argument.

claims.claim: when good deeds are spent the evil deeds that oppress a person take their place

1058.reading: Lights in the upper rooms dim, the dancing, drums and lutes tire and the singers' beat shrinks, and the fine city grows hushed like a sea whose waves have fallen.

1059.reading: The young men, their chests pressed to women's breasts and their garlands full of bees, loosen their clasp and fall asleep, their pleasures ended past all limit.
1059.event: The young men finish their night's pleasures and sleep.

1060.reading: The spirits that roam by night, having visited the toddy-shops, the frenzy-dance grounds and the streets where offerings are laid, are at last tired and asleep.
1060.nuance: The sense of line 3 and of the verb of 4 turns on rare words, and a reader should hold the reading loosely.
1060.event: The night spirits tire after their rounds and settle to sleep.

1061.reading: In the flowering grove the cock birds give the left wing to the young hen and spread the right over the chicks and sleep with their legs folded.
1061.nuance: The birds close the night's pictures with a family at rest, in contrast to the maiden's own wakeful longing.
1061.event: The cock birds shelter their mates and chicks as they sleep.

links.note: In 1040 the maiden prays that the sickness of birth leave her; in 1049 a friend says the love of a united pair outweighs even the state without birth and death.
links.teaches: The same eve holds two valuations of release, a bride's prayer and a friend's boast, and the poet leaves them standing side by side.

links.note: 1054 names the wedding day as the day to enjoy good deeds; 1057 uses the passing of good deeds and the coming of evil ones as a figure for night's darkness.
links.teaches: The same karmic words serve first for a bride's joy and then for the dread of night, so the story's fortune is read through deeds both times.

links.note: 1053 proposes to beg the moon to bring tomorrow near; 1056 shows the moon shrinking and sinking.
links.teaches: The moon she meant to petition simply sets, so the night she wished short is shown passing without her asking.

links.note: 1050 shows birds without mates as fire to the separated; 1061 shows paired birds sheltering mates and young as they sleep.
links.teaches: The birds that stand for separation in the friends' talk stand for union in the poet's closing picture, which gives the night a second reading.

links.note: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one can be sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; verse 1049 sets the lovers' union above the state without birth and death.
links.teaches: The Soolamani friend raises the Kural's comparison from a god's heaven to release itself, the goal her own Jain work teaches.

gains.a: The verse lacks a model for weighing love against the highest good, which the Kural's open question gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where the thing weighed against love is release from birth, not a heaven.

links.note: Naladiyar 51 says that, as darkness rushes in when a lamp's oil runs out, evil takes its stand when good deeds are spent; 1057 sets the passing of good deeds beside the thickening of darkness at night.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar teaches the lamp-and-darkness figure as a rule; the epic turns it into a description of night, which shows how common the figure was.

gains.a: The verse gives the darkness-and-deeds figure without a rule, which the quatrain's lamp and oil supply.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a scene in which the darkness is a real night around a sleeping city.

links.note: Kural 1183 says love has taken the woman's grace and modesty and left sickness and pallor; verse 1045 shows a maiden who tries to hide her sickness and is betrayed by her pallor.
links.teaches: The epic shows the moment when modesty tries to hold and pallor breaks it, a step the couplet only reports after the fact.

gains.a: The verse lacks a statement that pallor is the price paid for modesty, which the couplet states.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a maiden before marriage who still has her modesty and is losing it.

links.note: Naladiyar 23 says the wedding drums of one hall can be the funeral drums for the bridegroom the same day; verse 1052 reports a drum sounding tomorrow's wedding.
links.teaches: Read beside the quatrain, the drum of joy carries the warning of the same drum's other use, which the epic's happy scene does not say itself.

gains.a: The verse lacks any thought that the festive drum could mean loss, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a drum that is only the announcement of a coming wedding, with no loss in the story.

source_issues: Verse 1039: the stanza printed as eight half-lines and was repaired to four lines; lines 2 and 3 are near-repeats and the sentence is broken.
Verses 1047 to 1054: the friends' speeches are not marked by any speaker word beyond ஒருத்தி, and the word division is broken in several lines (1048, 1050, 1052 to 1054).
Verse 1060: rare words make the second half uncertain.
